extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of philosophy/history of science; practicing scientists interested in theory-choice and scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and values that scientists and scientific communities use to evaluate, choose between, and practice scientific theories, including the role of exemplars and tacit knowledge in training and persuasion in revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction accuracy and quantitative preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictions should be accurate; quantitative predictions are preferable to qualitative ones; whatever the margin of permissible error, it should be consistently satisfied in a given field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that predictive success is a primary value. The margin of permissible error should be a stable, community-recognized standard within a field; quantitative specificity is favored over vague qualitative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit puzzle-formulation and solution (problem-solving capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories must, first and foremost, permit puzzle-formulation and solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good theory supplies concrete problems and methods for solving them (it makes puzzles) and thereby provides the basis for normal scientific practice and training through exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, self-consistency, and plausibility (compatibility with other theories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible [theories] should be simple, self-consistent, and plausible, compatible, that is, with other theories currently deployed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard evaluative values; they can be weighted differently by individuals and communities. Simplicity here includes parsimony of assumptions; consistency includes both internal logical consistency and agreement with established parts of the disciplinary matrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal and external consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal and external consistency are important values for judging theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal consistency: lack of contradictions within the theory. External consistency: compatibility with other accepted theories and empirical results. The author notes earlier insufficiency of attention to these in his original text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social usefulness (optional value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science should (or need not) be socially useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social usefulness is identified as a possible evaluative value but not treated as primary; its importance may vary by community and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared values as community determinants (stability vs variability of application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared values (e.g., judgments of accuracy, simplicity, plausibility) may be widely shared but applied differently by individuals; accuracy judgments are relatively stable, whereas simplicity/consistency/plausibility vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition that the same named value can be applied differently by different scientists; evaluation must account for the distributive role of shared values in risk-taking and collective decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplars (paradigms) as central evaluative/training tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplars are the concrete problem-solutions students encounter (laboratory problems, textbook end-of-chapter problems, technical problem-solutions in the literature) that illustrate how the job is to be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplars supply the fine-structure of a community's practice and train novices to 'see' situations in the group-licensed way; the presence, quality, and extensiveness of exemplars are a basis for judging a theory's practical utility and pedagogical fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to foster tacit knowledge and perceptual 'seeing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge embedded in exemplars produces tacit knowledge: abilities to recognize relevant similarities and to construct appropriate versions of law-sketches in varied situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valuable theory/practice is one that, through exemplars and training, embeds systematic but not necessarily rule-expressible abilities (tacit knowledge) in practitioners; this is essential for effective problem identification and solution even if not fully articulable as explicit criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to reduction to explicit rules (limitations of rule-based criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquired similarity relations and tacit recognition should not be reconstructed simply as a set of explicit rules; seeking full criteria for similarity may be misguided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should not assume that all competent judgment can be reduced to traceable rules; many perceptual and interpretive competencies are involuntary, trained, and only subsequently analyzable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness, scope, and other traditional philosophical values
rubrics_metrics.description: Values usually listed by philosophers of science—accuracy, simplicity, fruitfulness, and the like—function as reasons in theory choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These act as values rather than algorithmic criteria; different scientists may weigh them differently. 'Fruitfulness' typically refers to the capacity to generate new problems, methods, or research programs; 'scope' to breadth of phenomena explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasiveness and community conversion (role of persuasion in theory choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Superiority of one theory to another cannot always be proved in debate; each party must try, by persuasion, to convert the other, and the community's persuasion determines effective choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because debates over theory-choice lack the fixed premises and rules of formal proof, persuasive force—how well arguments and exemplars convert colleagues—is a decisive evaluative factor. Good reasons can exist but function as values applied variably; the community, not an algorithm, settles disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability under potential incommensurability
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties to debates may see certain experimental or observational situations differently, attach terms differently, and therefore communicate only partially; yet persuasion and shared aspects of vocabulary enable conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of a theory should consider how its practitioners can communicate their observations and arguments to others whose perceptual/interpretive training differs; practical communicability and the ability to translate exemplars matter where incommensurability arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-level decision and distribution of risk
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no neutral algorithm for theory-choice; it is the community of specialists rather than its individual members that makes the effective decision, and the use of shared values may serve to distribute risk and assure long-term success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should account for communal mechanisms (training, exemplars, persuasion) that make a theory viable for a specialist community, including how communal adoption spreads risk-taking for revolutionary proposals.
